newsitem.title: UK: T&N may still see way to buy Kolbenschmidt.
newsitem.headline: T&N may still see way to buy Kolbenschmidt.

text.p: Industry sources say the jury is still out on whether British firm T&N Plc regards the sale of a key stake in Kolbenschmidt AG to a third party on Wednesday a help or hindrance in its own quest to take over the German pistons maker.
Earlier German defence and engineering group Rheinmetall AG said it was acquiring a 24.99 percent stake from Commerzbank AG.
"We have no comment to make at this stage...Rheinmetall is of course a very good company," a spokeswoman for T&N said.
But industry sources said it was possible that in time Rheinmetall's move could prove to be friendly to T&N's own long-running battle to combine its pistons business with Kolbenschmidt's.

Analysts said a hidden agenda would not be surprising but they could not see immediately how the British firm and Rheinmetall strategies could fit together. "I don't know is the short answer. We are all a bit baffled," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
T&N Plc holds options on a similar-sized stake with Germany's Metallbank, priced at 17 marks a share.

The British firm once had an option on buying the stake held by Commerzbank but the bank refused to renew the option which lapsed at the end of last year after the German Cartel Office banned T&N from buying into Kolbenschmidt .
But T&N says it still retains title to half of any profits Commerzbank makes from selling the shares at over 14 marks a share.
It also expects a Berlin appeals court to give it the formal go-ahead this week to exercise the Metallbank option on 25 percent of Kolbenschmidt.
T&N's chairman Sir Colin Hope told Reuters earlier he also expected the court to announce by Friday that it would review the ban on T&N making a bid for the company.

Hope said lawyers for the company were told by the court last week that it believed the Cartel Office had treated T&N unfairly and therefore it would call for a review of the whole case. Hope also said he was looking at the possibilities of forming a joint venture with Kolbenschmidt if a takeover proved impossible, to overtake Mahle as the market leader for engine pistons.

"Our whole approach has been to try to put together a package which will ensure that either by way of acquisition or by way of perhaps some joint ventures or some restructuring of the businesses we end up in that world leadership business," he said.
Hope said talks had been continuing with Kolbenschmidt, despite the battle with the Cartel Office.

"It's been an ongoing dialogue," he said. "They have always argued that they would not publicly say so because the Kartellamt would never let them do it. Now, of course, if the Kartellamt decision is being opened up again then it should open up that position again."
